methodological_rigor.justification: The study uses a well-described EV isolation and ExoCounter workflow, evaluates multiple lectins, applies SVM-based selection, and reports two PDAC cohorts plus other cancer comparisons. Diagnostic performance is quantified with ROC AUCs, confidence intervals, DeLong comparison with CA19-9, PR-AUC, calibration, and decision-curve analyses. Limitations are important: all samples were from established PDAC cases, the same normal controls were used for SVM training and validation, cohorts were all Japanese and not matched, CA19-9 was measured only in a subset, and analytical reproducibility studies remain future work.

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: This diagnostic case-control biomarker study compares PDAC serum samples with normal and other-cancer controls, so Oxford LoE is best classified as 3b. The clinical relevance is substantial because early PDAC detection is a major unmet need and the Jacalin/ABA EV model reports AUC 0.870 for stage I disease and outperforms CA19-9 in the tested subset. Clinical readiness is limited because the study did not test asymptomatic screening populations, benign pancreatic disease controls, or fully independent normal-control validation.

reporting_quality.justification: STARD is applicable because this is a diagnostic accuracy study. The manuscript describes sample sources, EV preparation, assay procedures, candidate lectin selection, machine-learning model inputs, ROC metrics, stage-specific performance, and other-cancer discrimination. Reporting remains incomplete for a diagnostic test because patient selection is case-control rather than intended-use screening, the same NC samples were reused across training and validation, no public data/code are described, and analytical validation measures such as reproducibility, dilution linearity, spike-in recovery, and freeze-thaw stability are deferred.

novelty_literature.justification: The study is novel in combining serum EV counting with optimized lectin glycan recognition and SVM selection to identify Jacalin/ABA as a two-lectin PDAC diagnostic signature. It builds on the authors' prior ExoCounter and ABA/ACA EV work, so it is not wholly first-in-class, but the optimized Jacalin/ABA combination and validation across a second PDAC cohort are meaningful extensions. The inclusion of early-stage PDAC and other cancer comparisons adds empirical novelty.

writing_presentation.justification: The abstract is clear and quantitatively summarizes the diagnostic AUCs and stage I result. The methods give enough operational detail on antibodies, lectins, EV isolation, ExoCounter measurement, CA19-9 ELISA, and SVM analysis to understand the workflow. The results follow the experimental sequence logically, and the discussion provides an unusually detailed list of limitations that appropriately tempers the screening claims.

key_strengths: Addresses the major unmet need of early PDAC blood-based detection.
Combines a defined EV-counting platform with systematic lectin screening and SVM optimization.
Reports strong diagnostic AUCs across two cohorts and stage I PDAC performance.
Compares against CA19-9 and includes PR-AUC, calibration, and decision-curve analyses.
Explicitly identifies key validation and analytical-performance gaps.
key_concerns: Case-control design with established PDAC cases does not establish screening performance.
The same normal controls were used for SVM training and validation.
Cohorts were all Japanese and clinicopathological backgrounds were not matched.
Specificity remains uncertain against lung cancer and benign pancreatic diseases.
No public analysis code or raw data availability is described.
chief_reviewer.rationale: This is the strongest paper in the batch because it pairs a clear diagnostic need with an assay platform, validation cohort, and quantitative performance analyses. Tier 2 is plausible, but only with major revisions or added validation addressing control reuse, intended-use populations, and analytical reproducibility.
